data.title: Hidden Files, Processes and Windows
data.summary: The sample sets the hidden/system file attributes, uses a leading dot or reserved naming convention, or otherwise marks its dropped files and directories so they do not appear in a default directory listing.
data.description:
This is a cheap, user-mode technique — no kernel component is needed, only standard file
attribute APIs or naming conventions the shell happens to suppress by default — but it is
effective against exactly the casual review it is aimed at: an analyst or user browsing
Explorer or a default `dir`/`ls` will not see the dropped files at all. It is frequently
combined with a plausible-looking name (a dotted system-folder name on macOS/Linux, a
name resembling a legitimate Windows component) rather than relying on hiding alone.
data.recommendation:
* List directory contents with hidden and system files shown explicitly (dir /a, ls -la) rather than relying on default tooling during triage.
* Check hidden locations against a known-good baseline for the OS and version in use; legitimate hidden files follow predictable patterns.
* Treat a hidden file with a name resembling a legitimate component as higher suspicion than an openly visible one with the same name.
data.short_recommendation: List directories with hidden and system files shown explicitly; default tooling will not surface this.

mitre_techniques.procedure: Set the hidden and system file attributes on its dropped payload and configuration files immediately after writing them.

mbc_techniques.implementation: Dropped files carried the hidden and system attributes and a name resembling a legitimate OS component.
